stimulus.text:
“Among the numerous advantages promised by a well constructed Union, none deserves to be more accurately developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction. . . . By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community. . . . Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens.”

—Publius (James Madison), Federalist No. 10, New York Daily Advertiser, November 22, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

stem: What does the title page of The Federalist, shown with this essay, tell the reader about the essays' purpose?

options.text: They were written against the new Constitution, to stop ratification
options.misconception: The title page says the essays were written in favour of the new Constitution, not against it.

options.text: They were the official record of the debates at Philadelphia
options.misconception: The essays were newspaper arguments for ratification, not the Convention's record; Madison's notes are that record.

options.text: They were written by the king's ministers to defend British rule
options.misconception: The essays were written by Americans as Publius to defend the Constitution, not by British ministers.

options.text: They were written in favour of the new Constitution

rationales.D: The title page states the essays were written in favour of the new Constitution, as agreed upon by the Federal Convention, September 17, 1787, so their purpose was to defend the proposed Constitution.
rationales.A: The title page says in favour of the new Constitution, the opposite of this claim.
rationales.B: The essays argued a public case in newspapers. Background: the Convention's record is Madison's private notes.
rationales.C: Background: the authors were Hamilton, Madison, and Jay writing as Publius, not British ministers.
rationales.general:
1. Read the title page: A Collection of Essays, Written in Favour of the New Constitution.
2. It adds the date the Convention agreed upon it: September 17, 1787.
3. Background: the essays were first newspaper pieces, then collected into two volumes in 1788.
4. So the book's purpose is stated on its own title page: to defend the proposed Constitution.
Remember: a title page states a book's purpose, so read it as evidence.
